comments.text:
25:30 That is honestly a pretty hard leap and I think it's done for TV show reasons. Like we don't know if this patient has a kidney disease, is a type 1 diabetic, is on diuretics for some reason, etc etc. There's lots of causes of hypokalemia and they just ran with one. That's not how that works. Great, he has insanely low potassium, get started on the correct protocol to bring that up to non-almost dead levels and the ICU can figure out what the cause is because they're going to be in the hospital for several days at minimum. 

For people who don't know, electrolytes like sodium or potassium levels in blood get that out of whack they have to be adjusted extremely cautiously and slowly because too much too fast will literally kill the patient. The DKA patient is going through similar things because that's commonly part of diabetic ketoacidosis. Certain things work against others, some work with others like magnesium, it's an entire class and learning process. Patients are monitored and checked regularly to make sure nothing is getting more out of whack and a really good idea for most, if not all, diabetic patients is to have a CMP labwork done regularly which checks these markers(and several others) to make sure you're not getting into any danger zones and if you are, please speak to your doctor about them. A potassium level below 3 is considered extremely dangerous. 1 for most people would straight up be dead.

Dr Mike, You mentioned that patients struggle with lifestyle changes. I can definitely relate personally, the two biggest barriers for me are pain and expense.

I have fibromyalgia, sciatica, chronic groin and hip issues, ADHD, and ASD. Walking is a real challenge—some days I can barely get around the house, other days even 50 meters can make me feel sick from the pain. Sometimes I struggle just walking to the shops and back, having to stop and lean on things. I’m only 36, and my GP even referred me for a wheelchair assessment.

Mentally, it’s tough. I used to cycle 400 miles a week and work 60–100 hour weeks. I’m definitely not lazy, but it’s hard to “just get active” when every movement hurts. 

And because doctors often don’t fully understand the level of pain or assume you’re just seeking medication help can be minimal. 

Never mind the there’s a lot of gaslighting around fibromyalgia, which is a diagnosis of exclusion with no definitive test. I genuinely had a physiotherapist tell me, “I normally dismiss patients with fibromyalgia because, if it’s just a GP diagnosis, I don’t even take it seriously—but since you were diagnosed by rheumatology, I’ll take it.

Often the Gp response is just YouTube links for CBT or antidepressants. If I weren’t in pain, I probably wouldn’t be depressed—go figure. It's taken years of fighting for medicine and tbh it's useless. 

Expense is another huge factor. Eating healthier is recommended, but it’s expensive. Processed food is cheap and convenient, even if it’s full of ingredients our grandparents never saw. 

A family dinner with processed food might cost £5, whereas a healthy, from-scratch dinner could be £20. 

Burnout, diet, and access to affordable nutrition play a huge role in chronic illness and disability.

Of course, there’s more to it than this, but unless someone like “Max from New Amsterdam” shows up with a magic wand, I fear chronic illness and disability will continue to rise. 

For context, in Japan, about 7% of the population is affected, whereas here in the UK, around 25% live with chronic illness or disability.
